# Trust is part of distribution {#sec-distribution}

A package needs to look trustworthy to the operating system before it can look trustworthy to
a user. Signing connects the package to its publisher and detects later changes.

## Sign the final artifact {#sec-signing}

Archive symbols and remove application debug information during deployment, then sign every
contained binary, then sign the installer or disk image. A file
changed after signing loses its signature.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    B[Build] --> T[Test] --> D[Deploy and archive symbols] --> S[Sign application]
    S --> P[Package] --> SP[Sign package] --> N[Notarize on macOS]
```

## macOS needs notarization {#sec-sign-macos}

Outside the App Store, use a Developer ID certificate, the hardened runtime, notarization, and
stapling. Keep the certificate and notarization credentials in the CI secret store, never in
the repository.

Notarization submits the signed app or package to Apple for automated checks. Stapling attaches
the resulting ticket, so Gatekeeper can check it when the user is offline. The template's
release workflow builds packages; it does not configure signing or notarization for you.

## Windows uses Authenticode {#sec-sign-windows}

Sign executables and installers with an Authenticode certificate and a timestamp. The timestamp
keeps a signature valid after the certificate expires. Use a hardware-backed or cloud signing
service for CI keys.

## Linux ships an AppImage {#sec-linux-package}

The Linux release workflow produces an x86-64 `.AppImage`. CPack stages the application under
`usr/` in an AppDir. Qt 6.12's deployment script adds QML imports, Qt libraries, and plugins,
including SVG, X11, Wayland, and the offscreen platform used by tests. Linuxdeploy then
collects further dependencies and fixes their runtime paths. Its bundled AppImage output
plugin builds the final image. No separate linuxdeploy Qt plugin is needed.

On x86-64 Linux, install linuxdeploy using the checksum-verified download
commands in `.github/workflows/release.yml`, then add their directory to `PATH`:

```sh
export PATH="$PWD/.cache/linuxdeploy:$PATH"
cmake --workflow --preset release
```

The workflow pins a tagged linuxdeploy release, including its AppImage output plugin.
Packaging requires `patchelf` and a shared Qt 6.12 installation with X11 and Wayland support.
The project's vcpkg Qt feature provides that Qt configuration. The packaging tool runs through
AppImage's extraction fallback, so building needs no FUSE mount.

An AppImage still depends on the host's Linux ABI, glibc, graphics drivers, and display
services. The Ubuntu 24.04 build establishes that baseline; it does not promise support for
older distributions. Test hardware rendering and desktop integration on the systems you support.
Users can extract the image with `--appimage-extract`, replace its dynamic Qt libraries,
and run `squashfs-root/AppRun`. Notices are in `usr/bin/licenses/` inside the image.
Its `system-docs` link exposes linuxdeploy's system-library notices; `common` contains the
shared license texts referenced by Debian and Ubuntu copyright files.

## Stores trade control for services {#sec-stores}

A store handles discovery, trust, and updates, but adds its own sandbox, review process, and
package rules. Choose it when those services are worth the platform constraints.
